extra.message: SQL Injection in Login Authentication

metadata.citation: query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '{username}' AND password = '{password}'"
metadata.proof: SOURCE: form.username.data and form.password.data (lines 162-163) are user-controlled POST form fields with StringField (no sanitization). SINK: The formatted string is passed to conn.execute(query) at line 173. An attacker can submit username=' OR '1'='1' -- to bypass authentication entirely and log in as the first user (admin), gaining access to the entire application.

extra.message: SQL Injection in Comment Search

metadata.citation: query = f"SELECT * FROM comments WHERE content LIKE '%{search_term}%'"
metadata.proof: SOURCE: form.search.data (line 243) is a StringField with no input validation. SINK: The f-string is interpolated directly into cursor.execute(query) at line 249. An attacker can submit ' OR '1'='1 to dump all comments, or chain UNION SELECT to exfiltrate the users table (passwords, roles).

extra.message: Insecure Deserialization via pickle.loads

metadata.proof: SOURCE: form.data.data (line 433) is a user-controlled StringField containing arbitrary base64-encoded data. SINK: base64.b64decode(data) (line 435) then pickle.loads(decoded) (line 436). Pickle deserialization of untrusted data allows arbitrary code execution on the server by crafting a malicious __reduce__ payload.

extra.message: Unrestricted File Upload

metadata.proof: SOURCE: request.files['file'] (line 319) accepts any file with no content-type or extension validation. SINK: file.save(file_path) (line 322) saves the file to static/uploads/, which is served by send_from_directory via the /uploads/<filename> route (line 339). The route is also @csrf.exempt (line 304), removing CSRF protection. An attacker can upload HTML/JS files for stored XSS, or if the server allows execution (e.g., CGI configured on the uploads directory), achieve RCE.

extra.message: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)

metadata.proof: SOURCE: form.url.data (line 381) is a user-controlled URL with no allowlist/blocklist validation. SINK: requests.get(url, timeout=2) (line 384) makes an arbitrary HTTP request from the server. An attacker can target internal services (localhost:5000, cloud metadata endpoints like 169.254.169.254), read internal file contents, or probe internal network services.

extra.message: XML External Entity (XXE) Injection

metadata.proof: SOURCE: form.xml_data.data (line 406) is user-controlled XML text. SINK: ET.fromstring(xml_data) (line 409 and again at line 417) parses XML with the default parser. On Python < 3.7.1, external entities like SYSTEM 'file:///etc/passwd' will be resolved, exposing server files. Additionally, lxml is present in requirements.txt which can be used as an alternative parser with entity resolution enabled.

extra.message: DOM-based Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)

metadata.proof: SOURCE: window.location.hash (line 138) is attacker-controlled via URL fragment like #message=<script>alert(1)</script>. The hash value is extracted and parsed via URLSearchParams at lines 139-140. SINK: innerHTML assignment at line 143 injects the unsanitized message directly into the DOM, executing arbitrary JavaScript. No sanitization (e.g., textContent or DOMPurify) is applied.

extra.message: Predictable Session Token / Broken Authentication

metadata.proof: SOURCE: The session_id is derived from the username with a fixed suffix _auth_123 (line 190). It is stored in the session (line 191) and exposed as a cookie (line 195). The broken-auth endpoint (line 466) accepts any POST with matching session_token compared to session.get('session_id'). An attacker can guess admin_auth_123 and authenticate as admin, bypassing password verification entirely.

extra.message: Hardcoded Weak Secret Key

metadata.proof: The Flask SECRET_KEY is hardcoded at line 25 as the weak string 'secure-secret-key-12345'. This key is used to sign session cookies (Flask's session cookie). An attacker who knows this key can forge arbitrary session cookies, impersonate any user (including admin), and bypass all authentication. The key is also stored in the source code repository, making it accessible to anyone with read access.

metadata.proof: Passwords are stored as plaintext in the SQLite database (users table). The admin password is 'password' (line 96) and user2 password is 'password2' (line 99). No hashing (bcrypt, PBKDF2, argon2) is applied. SQL injection in the login (line 165) or comment search (line 247) allows an attacker to dump all credentials in cleartext.

extra.message: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) on Transfer via GET

metadata.proof:
SOURCE: The /transfer endpoint accepts GET requests (line 274) with the amount as a query parameter (line 275). No Origin/Referer validation or anti-CSRF token is checked. SINK: At line 286, a GET request triggers the transfer logic and records it as successful. A malicious page can auto-submit a GET request via /
to transfer funds without user consent, and the app explicitly provides a malicious_csrf_example.html page (line 301) to demonstrate the attack.

extra.message: CSRF Protection Exempted on File Upload

metadata.proof: The /upload endpoint is decorated with @csrf.exempt (line 304), disabling Flask-WTF's CSRF protection. Combined with unrestricted file upload (CWE-434), this allows an attacker to craft a CSRF form that uploads a malicious file to the server when a logged-in victim visits the attacker's page, achieving blind upload without the victim's consent.

extra.message: Hardcoded Flask SECRET_KEY Enables Session Forgery

metadata.proof: SOURCE: static hardcoded string in source code at line 25. SINK: Flask's SECRET_KEY used to cryptographically sign session cookies. Anyone with access to the source (public repository) can forge valid Flask session cookies, impersonate any user, and bypass all authentication. The key 'secure-secret-key-12345' is trivially guessable even without source access.

extra.message: Predictable Session Token Generation Enables Session Hijacking

metadata.proof: SOURCE: user['username'] is known or guessable (admin, user2). SINK: session_id derived from fixed pattern `username_auth_123` at line 190, stored in session at line 191, and set as cookie vuln_session_id at line 195. The /broken-auth endpoint at line 472 validates submitted_token against session['session_id'], meaning an attacker who knows a victim's username can predict the session_id and bypass the broken-auth challenge. The fixed suffix '_auth_123' makes the token space trivial to enumerate.

extra.message: IDOR: Unauthorized Access to Arbitrary User Profiles via user_id Parameter

metadata.citation: user = conn.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", (user_id,)).fetchone()
metadata.proof: SOURCE: URL path parameter user_id at /profile/<int:user_id> (line 339). SINK: Database query at line 345 returns the full user record (including password, email, role fields) which is passed to the template at line 396 regardless of ownership. While the code detects IDOR at line 356 to award a CTF flag, the user data is still returned to the requester. Any authenticated user can view any other user's sensitive data by changing the URL.

extra.message: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) in API Endpoint /api/user/<int:user_id>

metadata.citation: return jsonify({"id": user['id'], "username": user['username'], "email": user['email'], "role": user['role'], "flag": "CTF{bola_success}"})
metadata.proof: SOURCE: URL path parameter user_id (line 608) — attacker-controlled. SINK: jsonify response at line 619 exposes id, username, email, role, and flag for ANY user. The endpoint checks authentication at line 610 but performs NO authorization check — the condition at line 617 (user_id != logged_in_user['id']) only controls whether to update progress, but the data is returned regardless when that condition is met. Any authenticated user can fetch any other user's PII via GET /api/user/1.

extra.message: Active Debug Mode Exposes Werkzeug Debugger with Potential RCE

metadata.proof: SOURCES: (1) debug=True at line 661 enables the Werkzeug interactive debugger which renders a stack trace and a Python REPL console on any unhandled exception. (2) The debugger PIN is computed from easily-leaked machine attributes (MAC address, machine ID via /proc). If the XXE vulnerability (line 407) is used to read /etc/machine-id or /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id, the attacker can compute the debugger PIN and execute arbitrary Python code, leading to full server compromise. Simply causing the application to error opens the console.

extra.message: Missing Authorization on /api/flag Endpoint

metadata.proof: SOURCE: Any HTTP request (unauthenticated) to /api/flag. SINK: Returns the hardcoded flag at line 624. The endpoint performs NO authentication or session check — no 'if user not in session' guard, unlike every other route in the application. An unauthenticated attacker can simply GET /api/flag and receive the flag. This also constitutes CWE-200 (Information Exposure) by leaking application secrets without any access control.

extra.message: CSRF Protection Exempted on /csrf Settings Page

metadata.proof: SOURCE: Attacker-crafted HTML form on a malicious site performing a cross-origin POST to /csrf with email=attacker@evil.com. SINK: The @csrf.exempt decorator at line 538 disables Flask-WTF CSRF token validation for the /csrf route, and the route processes form.email.data at line 554 to update the user's email without verifying the request origin. Any cross-site request forgery attack can modify the user's email setting. Distinct from the upload CSRF exemption at line 304.

extra.message: Information Exposure via Raw Database Error Messages in Login

metadata.proof: SOURCE: Malformed SQL injection payload in the login form (username/password fields). SINK: error = f"Database error: {str(e)}" at line 203 renders the raw sqlite3 exception message (e.g., table names, column names, query structure) directly into the login.html template via the error variable. This leaks backend implementation details to the attacker, aiding further attack development.

extra.message: Vulnerable Session Cookie Set Without Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite Flags

metadata.proof: On login success, a 'vuln_session_id' cookie is set via set_cookie() with no Secure, HttpOnly, or SameSite attributes. The predictable session ID (format: '{username}_auth_123') is transmitted in cleartext since the app runs on HTTP (no TLS) with debug=True. An attacker who obtains the cookie value via network sniffing, XSS, or CSRF can replay it to hijack the session.

extra.message: Hardcoded Credentials File Exposed on Filesystem

metadata.proof: A plaintext credentials file passwords.txt is stored at python/hackable/passwords.txt. The app's SSRF endpoint (/ssrf) accepts arbitrary URLs via requests.get(url) and returns the response text, enabling an attacker to read this file via file:/// scheme. The file contains two credential pairs (admin:admin123, user1:password123) that can be used to log in or fed into credential-stuffing attacks.

extra.message: Sensitive Flag File Exposed on Filesystem — Readable via SSRF

metadata.proof: A CTF flag file flag.txt is stored at python/hackable/flag.txt in plaintext. The SSRF endpoint (/ssrf) accepts arbitrary URLs via requests.get(url) and returns the response text, enabling an attacker to read this file via file:/// scheme. This exposes a secret flag that should not be stored on disk in plaintext.

extra.message: SQL Query and User Input Logged to stdout

metadata.proof: The full SQL query string (containing interpolated username and password from user-controlled form fields) is printed to stdout via print(). The query is constructed as f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '{username}' AND password = '{password}'", so the user's password appears in cleartext in server logs accessible to operators and monitoring systems.

extra.message: Session User and Database Records Logged to stdout

metadata.proof: In the profile route, the session username (print(f"Session user: {session['user']}")) and the entire database user record (print(f"Target user: {user}")) are printed to stdout. This leaks internal state — including all user columns from SELECT * — to anyone with access to server logs. If the schema ever included a password column, it would be logged in cleartext.

extra.message: Referer Header Logged to stdout

metadata.proof: The Referer header from incoming HTTP requests is printed to stdout in the transfer route. The Referer may contain sensitive information such as session tokens, internal URLs, or query parameters, leaking user browsing context to server logs.

extra.message: Log Actions Printed to stdout Including User and Details

metadata.proof: The log_action function in database.py prints every logged action (timestamp, user, action, details) to stdout via print(). The 'details' field contains user-generated text and descriptive strings about exploits performed (e.g., 'CSRF exploit completed for transfer, Amount: 100'), leaking every user's activity trace including sensitive details like transfer amounts.

extra.message: Missing Rate Limiting on Login Endpoint Enables Brute-Force Attacks

metadata.proof: The login route (/) at line 153 has no rate-limiting, account-lockout, or CAPTCHA mechanism. An attacker can submit thousands of password guesses per minute via automated scripts. Since passwords are stored in plaintext and the SQL query is injectable, a brute-force or dictionary attack can trivially compromise all accounts.

extra.message: Missing Rate Limiting on /broken-auth Session-Validation Endpoint

metadata.proof: The /broken-auth POST endpoint at line 464 accepts a submitted_token from the form and compares it against the predictable session_id (format: '{username}_auth_123'). There is no rate limiting, so an attacker can brute-force the session ID for any user. Because the session ID format is known and trivially guessable (e.g., 'admin_auth_123'), this enables session hijacking.

extra.message: Flask Session Cookie Not Configured with Secure Flag

metadata.citation:
app = Flask(__name__)
app.config['SECRET_KEY'] = 'secure-secret-key-12345'
app.config['UPLOAD_FOLDER'] = 'static/uploads'
csrf = CSRFProtect(app)
metadata.proof: The Flask application does not set SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE in app.config. Flask's default session cookie lacks the Secure flag, making it transmitted over plain HTTP connections where it can be intercepted via network sniffing. The app runs on port 5000 with debug=True and no TLS, so session cookies are sent in cleartext.

extra.message: Application Bound to 0.0.0.0 Exposes Server to All Network Interfaces

metadata.proof: The app is bound to 0.0.0.0 (all interfaces) with debug=True, making it accessible from any network interface including external ones if the firewall permits. This widens the attack surface beyond localhost, potentially allowing remote attackers to reach all vulnerable endpoints and access Flask's debugger which can execute arbitrary code.

                user = conn.execute(query).fetchone()

metadata.proof: SOURCE: User-controlled integer via form (user_id at line 488) flows into a raw SQL f-string at line 491 with no request throttling. The endpoint measures elapsed query time (lines 492-494) and rewards delays >2s, enabling automated time-based blind SQLi extraction. There is no rate limiter, token bucket, or CAPTCHA on this POST endpoint — an attacker can script hundreds of requests/second to exfiltrate the database character-by-character.

extra.message: Information Exposure via Raw SQL Error Message in Comment Search

metadata.proof: SOURCE: Untrusted user input via form.search.data (line 244) is interpolated into a raw SQL query at line 248: f"SELECT * FROM comments WHERE content LIKE '%{search_term}%'". SINK: When the query fails due to crafted input, the raw database exception (including SQL syntax details, table structure hints, and DB engine info) is reflected verbatim to the user at line 256 via error = f"Error executing query: {str(e)}". This leaks internal database details to attackers during reconnaissance.

extra.message: Missing Authentication on /uploads/<filename> — Unauthenticated File Access

metadata.proof: SOURCE: Any unauthenticated user can request /uploads/<filename> with no session requirement. SINK: The route at line 332-333 serves arbitrary files from UPLOAD_FOLDER via send_from_directory() without any if 'user' not in session guard. Combined with the unrestricted file upload (which allows .php uploads), this enables unauthenticated RCE by requesting a previously uploaded PHP webshell, and unauthenticated data exfiltration of any uploaded file.

extra.message: Missing Authentication on /csrf-exploit Demo Page — Public CSRF Attack Tool

metadata.proof: SOURCE: Any unauthenticated visitor can access /csrf-exploit. SINK: The route at line 297-299 renders csrf_exploit.html (which contains an auto-submitting CSRF exploit form targeting the app's /transfer endpoint) with zero authentication checks. While the /transfer endpoint requires login, this page provides a ready-made weaponized CSRF payload to anyone on the internet, lowering the barrier for attackers who can trick authenticated users into visiting this URL to trigger unauthorized transfers.
